title: miniCTX: Neural Theorem Proving with (Long-)Contexts
abstract: We introduce miniCTX, a benchmark for evaluating neural theorem provers in real-world settings where proofs depend on new context. Our benchmark tests a model's ability to prove theorems given access to code from the theorem's repository, which contains necessary context for the proof.

sections.title: The Core Insight
sections.content: Imagine you're trying to prove a mathematical theorem. You need to understand the context, including definitions, lemmas, and comments. Context-dependent theorem proving is crucial in real-world applications. We argue that neural provers must operate in this realistic context-dependent setting.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content: Our benchmark, miniCTX, consists of 762 theorems from six projects, each with its own context. We use NTP-TOOLKIT to extract and annotate the data. The model is tasked with proving a theorem given access to the preceding file contents and metadata.

sections.title: Benchmark Results
sections.content: We evaluate several baselines on miniCTX, including file-tuned models and state-tactic models. The results show that file-tuned models outperform state-tactic models, with a performance boost of up to 16.41% (35.94% vs. 19.53%).

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content: Our work has significant implications for the development of neural theorem provers. By incorporating context, we can improve the performance and generalizability of these models. This can lead to more effective automated proof assistants for mathematicians.

sections.title: Key Innovations
sections.content: Our key contributions include the introduction of miniCTX, a benchmark for evaluating neural theorem provers in real-world settings, and NTP-TOOLKIT, a toolkit for extracting and annotating theorem proving data.

sections.title: Try It Yourself
sections.content: We provide an interactive environment for evaluating neural theorem provers on miniCTX. You can try out different models and explore the effects of context on theorem proving performance.
